strengths: Learning Sinkhorn initializations from adversarially generated marginals is a meaningful approach to amortizing repeated optimal transport computations without requiring a particular training dataset.

The Hilbert projective loss naturally handles the nonuniqueness of dual potentials. Proposition 4.3 provides a sound fixed-point residual argument supporting bootstrapped targets, which avoid computing fully converged training labels.

The reported initialization improvements are substantial within the tested setting. For example, Table 2 reduces mean iterations to reach 0.01 marginal violation from 47 to 3 on CIFAR and from 41 to 4 on LFW, versus 17 and 14 for Gaussian initialization. Evaluation includes four datasets, 500 samples per dataset, and five independent training runs for the convergence plots.

The manuscript provides pseudocode, architecture and hyperparameter details, a code link, and a generator-versus-noise ablation. Reporting marginal violations alongside distance errors strengthens the empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The central universality claim is not established for the implemented method. Theorem 4.1 requires equal input/output dimensions and a constrained Lipschitz constant, whereas the experiments use 392 latent dimensions to generate two 784-dimensional histograms and explicitly omit the Lipschitz constraint. The authors acknowledge these differences but still conclude that generator expressiveness cannot be a bottleneck. Moreover, full support of a hypothetical generator would not establish uniformly accurate predictions from finite training.

Theorem 4.1 also needs correction under its stated assumptions. ReLU makes q noninvertible and introduces singular probability mass on the boundary: with net=0 in one dimension, q=ReLU(λz) has an atom at zero. Thus the global density and inverse used in Appendix A are not defined as claimed. An interior, almost-everywhere density statement appears repairable, but the current proof cannot justify the theorem on the entire nonnegative orthant.

The evaluated objective is inconsistent across the manuscript. Algorithm 1 returns the transport cost ⟨C,Γ⟩, while Section 5.2 defines the reference value as the minimum of ⟨C,Γ⟩−εH(Γ). These quantities differ even at convergence, contrary to Section 3.3. The implementation may use a consistent convention, but the paper must specify which quantity was measured before its relative-error results and standalone regularized-OT-solver claim can be assessed reliably.

The closest learned baseline, Amos et al. (2022), is excluded based on an asserted failure outside its training distribution, without a direct comparison. Training that method on the same generated samples would help distinguish improvements from the sampling strategy versus the proposed loss and bootstrapping. The noise ablation does not resolve this comparison. The claim to be the first meta neural OT solver also overstates the distinction from the cited Meta Optimal Transport work.

The experiments demonstrate transfer across image datasets, but provide limited evidence for arbitrary marginals even within the stated fixed-cost setting. Controlled tests on concentrated, near-boundary, and otherwise non-image distributions are missing. Practical speedup is also incompletely established: Figure 8 omits Gaussian-initialization timings, and the manuscript does not specify reference-solver tolerances or how zero-valued test-image entries are treated. These gaps limit confidence in the broader accuracy, robustness, and efficiency conclusions.
